{"body":"## Summary

On macOS 26.3.1, every `entire` subcommand (including `entire --version`) can hang indefinitely if the system's `syspolicyd` is in a bad state. This silently blocks Claude Code's `SessionStart` hook, which in turn blocks Claude Code from starting in any repo where `entire hooks claude-code session-start` is wired in.

Mechanically this is a macOS bug, not a CLI bug — but the impact for `entire` users is severe (Claude Code becomes unusable across every enabled repo), and the workaround documented in #380 (`xattr -d com.apple.provenance`) no longer works on macOS 14+ because that attribute is now SIP-protected.

## Environment

- macOS 26.3.1 (25D2128), arm64
- entire 0.5.6 (c9fedb4b), installed via `brew install --cask entire`
- Standard `SessionStart` hook calling `entire hooks claude-code session-start`

## Symptom

- Claude Code hangs silently at session start
- `entire --version` from any shell hangs indefinitely
- Stale `entire` processes accumulate (in my case, 8 of them, oldest 18+ hours old, all in state `S` with 0% CPU)
- `sample <pid>` shows every one stuck in `_dyld_start` — the binary never reaches `main()`

## Root cause

`syspolicyd` was wedged. PID had been alive for 42 days, 4 hours.

Kernel:

```yaml
kernel: (AppleSystemPolicy) ASP: Security policy would not allow process: <pid>, /opt/homebrew/Caskroom/entire/0.5.6/entire
```

`syspolicyd` looping:

```yaml
syspolicyd: [com.apple.syspolicy.exec:default] Unable to initialize qtn_proc: 3
syspolicyd: [com.apple.syspolicy.exec:default] dispatch_mig_server returned 268435459
```

When `syspolicyd` can't init the quarantine subsystem, dyld stalls every new process that triggers a policy check.

## Fix

```sh
sudo kill <syspolicyd-pid>   # launchd respawns it within ~1s
```

`launchctl kickstart -k system/com.apple.security.syspolicy` does **not** work — SIP blocks it (`150: Operation not permitted while System Integrity Protection is engaged`). `kill` does work because SIP doesn't restrict signaling root processes.

## Suggested CLI improvements

1. **Self-imposed timeout in hook entry points.** `entire hooks claude-code session-start` should bound itself to ~5s. A wedged `syspolicyd` currently cascades into permanently broken Claude Code sessions; a timeout + stderr would degrade gracefully.
2. **Update troubleshooting docs.** The `xattr -d com.apple.provenance` advice from #380 doesn't work on current macOS. Include the `syspolicyd` diagnostic (kernel log signature + `kill <pid>`).
3. **`entire doctor` health probe.** Attempt a self-launch with a short timeout; if it hangs, surface the kernel log signature so users can diagnose this in minutes instead of hours.
","comments":[{"a":"MuskanPaliwal","b":"hi @ashtom and @basher83, I tried to reproduce this locally against the current release builds and couldn’t.

  Tested:

  - latest stable: `v0.6.1` / `774ee21`
  - latest nightly: `v0.6.2-nightly.202605160654.ddf1a331`

  For both binaries, I ran two probes with 5s timeouts:

  - `entire --version`
  - `entire hooks claude-code session-start` with Claude-style `SessionStart` stdin matching the hook schema

  Both completed successfully. The hook returned the expected JSON response:

  ```json
  {"systemMessage":"\n\nEntire CLI will link this conversation to your next commit."}
```

So I don’t think this is caused by Claude hook stdin parsing or the `session-start` handler itself.
The key clue is that `entire --version` also hangs in the reported environment, and the sample shows the process stuck in `_dyld_start`. That means the binary hasn’t reached Go `main()` yet, so Cobra, hook parsing, logging, and any internal Go timeout haven’t started. This points to a macOS launch / Gatekeeper / `syspolicyd` state issue surfacing through the Claude hook path. The reported recovery, killing the wedged `syspolicyd` process, fits that.
I think the right mitigation on our side is to make the production Claude `SessionStart` hook fail open using Claude Code’s native per-hook timeout. We can keep the existing hook command, but install it with a short timeout, likely 5 seconds. That keeps the timeout outside the child `entire` process, so if macOS stalls before Go `main()` starts, Claude Code can cancel the hook and continue startup instead of waiting indefinitely."},{"a":"basher83","b":"Update from the original reporter: hit this again on **2026-07-02** (macOS **26.5.1**, Apple silicon, entire **0.7.8** via Homebrew cask, seeded during the 0.7.7→0.7.8 cask upgrade). This time I ran a full discriminator/probe series before remediating, so I can now say considerably more about the mechanism than the April report. It confirms @MuskanPaliwal's triage — the hang is pre-`main()` and nothing inside the Go binary can bound it — and adds new mechanism detail that affects the fix's scope.

### Symptom recap

Every invocation of the installed binary hung indefinitely, including `entire version`. `sample` on a stuck `entire hooks claude-code session-start` showed **786/786 samples at `_dyld_start (in dyld) + 0`** — blocked in kernel image-activation/exec-authorization before any Go code runs. Impact: `git commit` hung in every entire-enabled repo (even `git commit --no-verify` — prepare-commit-msg/post-commit are outside `--no-verify`); `ps` showed **14 blocked `entire hooks …` processes** accumulated across Claude Code and Pi sessions.

### Probe ledger (each hypothesis falsified or confirmed by the next probe, never by assertion)

Exec guards used `perl -e 'alarm N; exec @ARGV'` (macOS has no `timeout`); exit 142 = SIGALRM = hang.

| Probe | Question | Result |
|---|---|---|
| p1 | Does a byte-identical `cp` copy (xattrs inherited) reproduce? | hang — control valid |
| p2 | Is quarantine the mechanism? | quarantine removed → **still hangs. Quarantine FALSIFIED** (consistent with the #380 workaround no longer working) |
| p3 | Do other new binaries hang on first exec? | fresh hello-world + fresh copy of node both run — **host machinery healthy** |
| p4 | Corrupt download / weird load commands? | `codesign` deep-verify valid, vanilla system dylibs — **corruption FALSIFIED** |
| p5 | Same bytes, no inherited xattrs? | runs instantly — **poison is file-attached state, not content** |
| p6 | Does fresh content at the install path fix it? | replacement **still hung at the install path** → path-level block discovered |
| p7 | Path-keyed or inode-keyed? | proven-running inode moved into the same dir → runs — path-string-linked |
| p8 | Path block persistent? | rename cycle + killing the 13 wedged exec-auth requests for that path → path healthy — **transient queued-auth amplifier** |
| p9 | Original file after full flush? | **still hangs at a new path** — the durable poison is the original file itself |

### Established facts

1. **The poison is attached to the specific installed file** (inode + protected xattrs), not its content: identical bytes (same sha256) in freshly created files run everywhere, including the Caskroom dir and the install path. Leading suspect: the SIP-protected `com.apple.provenance` record (value `010200C15D9C3C787F507C`, seeded at the cask-upgrade timestamp; survives `xattr -d`).
2. **Per-path queue amplifier** (new, and nasty): while wedged exec-auth requests for the install path were pending, **even healthy fresh files hung at that exact path**. Flushed by a rename cycle + killing the stuck processes. This means "reinstall it" can appear not to work until the queue drains — likely why remediation reports on this class are inconsistent.
3. **Recurred the same day with zero brew activity**, falsifying upgrade-window seeding as the sole trigger. (Working hypothesis: the preserved poisoned specimen sitting in the live Caskroom dir was itself a re-wedging vector; it's now defused — tarred, raw binary removed — and the next recurrence is decisive either way.)
4. Killing `syspolicyd` was not needed here. Working remediation: **fresh-content replacement at the install path + queue drain** (kill stuck `entire hooks` procs, rename-cycle the path). A fully hook-enabled `git commit` completed normally afterwards.

### What this means for the fix

The pre-`main()` locus means no in-process timeout can ever fire — the bound has to live in what entire *emits*, so PR #1237's direction (Claude Code's native per-hook `timeout`) is exactly right. But two scope notes from this occurrence:

1. **All Claude hooks need the timeout, not just SessionStart.** Most of the 14 blocked processes were `stop` / `session-end` flavors — every session leaked one on exit, silently.
2. **The generated git hooks have no watchdog at all.** `prepare-commit-msg`/`post-commit`/etc. wrap the invocation in `… 2>/dev/null || true`, which guards *failure* but not *hanging* — an exec-auth wedge never returns, so `git commit` hangs in every enabled repo and `--no-verify` doesn't help. A bounded invocation in `strategy/hooks.go`'s generated scripts would contain this (with care to preserve `pre-push`'s deliberate fail-closed OPF contract). Happy to open a follow-up PR for this if there's interest.

Interim guardrail I'm using host-side, in case it helps others on this issue:

```bash
perl -e 'alarm 5; exec @ARGV' /opt/homebrew/bin/entire version
```

### Evidence available

The poisoned specimen is preserved (tarball, sha256-recorded), along with `sample` output, xattr dumps, and verbatim transcripts of every probe above. Glad to share any of it here or in an Apple Feedback report — the specimen makes the hang reproducible on demand, which the earlier "cannot reproduce" attempts lacked.
"}],"state":"OPEN","title":"`entire` hangs in `_dyld_start` when `syspolicyd` is wedged, blocking Claude Code session-start hooks"}

content.text:
Short answer: the problem is still real, but this PR can't merge as written. I'd rewrite it on current `main` rather than rebase it.

**Why the problem still needs a fix**
- `main` deliberately sets no timeout on any of Entire's Claude hooks. The comment at `hooks.go:598` on `origin/main` says they all "keep Claude Code's default". So #1065 is not fixed anywhere else.
- The reporter hit it again on 2026-07-02 (macOS 26.5.1, entire 0.7.8). Their tests confirm your diagnosis: the process is stuck before `main()`, so nothing inside the binary can set a limit. They say the per-hook `timeout` in Claude's settings is "exactly right".
- One caveat: Claude Code already applies a default hook timeout, so "hangs forever" is too strong in the Claude path. What the PR really buys is a 5s failure instead of a long stall on every session start. That's still worth it, but the description should say it that way.

**Why the current PR won't work**
1. **Merge conflicts.** GitHub reports the PR as `CONFLICTING`, and its last update was 2026-07-03.
2. **It's built around `localDev`, which no longer exists.** Local-dev mode was removed in `a9a676e79` (2026-08-14). The `if !localDev` branch and the "leaves local-dev hook installs unchanged" claim are now dead code and a wrong claim.
3. **`main` already has `Timeout` on `ClaudeHookEntry`.** The `types.go` change would duplicate it.
4. **The reporter says the scope is too narrow:**
   - Most of the 14 stuck processes they found came from the `stop` and `session-end` hooks, not `session-start`.
   - The git hooks generated in `strategy/hooks.go` have no time limit at all. `|| true` covers a failing hook but not a hung one, so `git commit` hangs, even with `--no-verify`. They offered to send a follow-up PR for this.

**What I'd do**
- Close this PR and open a fresh one on `main` that:
  - sets `timeout: 5` on SessionStart;
  - adds the same backfill for existing installs.
- Probably also add timeouts to Stop and SessionEnd, but with a bigger budget than 5s, since those hooks do real work (condensing sessions, capturing transcripts). A 5s limit could kill a legitimate run.
- Leave the git-hook part to the reporter's offered follow-up, or file it as a separate issue.
- One small problem in the current code: the backfill overwrites any timeout a user set on Entire's own hook. Better to only fill it in when it's missing.

If you want, I can draft the rewrite proposal or a reply on the PR. I'll show you the text before posting anything.

content.text:
Fair challenge. The case for it is weaker than the PR makes it sound.

**What the fix actually buys**

It doesn't fix the bug. The hang is a macOS exec-authorization problem (`syspolicyd` / provenance state), and when it happens `entire` is broken whatever we do. All the timeout changes is how long Claude Code waits before giving up on the SessionStart hook. Claude Code already has a default hook timeout, so even without our change the hook stops eventually. The gain is "5 seconds" instead of "the default", per session start, only while the machine is in that state.

**Why that may not be worth much**
- **The user is stuck either way.** In the July report, `git commit` hung in every repo with Entire enabled, even with `--no-verify`. They had to diagnose and fix the macOS state no matter what. A faster Claude start doesn't remove that.
- **It's rare.** Both reports come from the same person on the same kind of machine, and neither you nor anyone else could reproduce it.
- **A short timeout has a real cost.** The first launch of a freshly upgraded binary can be slow while macOS scans it. A 5s limit could cut off a *healthy* session-start, and then the session silently doesn't get tracked. That trades a rare, loud failure for a more common, silent one.

**The real argument for it**

Claude Code is the user's main tool and Entire is a side tool. A side tool should never block the main one, and a 5s cap means a sick `entire` makes Claude slow rather than unusable. That's a reasonable principle. But here it only covers one of the places Entire can hang, and git commit still hangs.

**My take**

The PR isn't needed in its current form, and I wouldn't push hard to revive it. If you want to do something for #1065, these give more value for less risk:
- a troubleshooting doc entry for the `_dyld_start` symptom, with the fix the reporter found;
- possibly an `entire doctor` check that launches the binary with a time limit and reports when it hangs.

If maintainers still want the timeout, use a generous value (for example 30s) rather than 5s, so slow first launches don't get killed.

One thing I didn't verify: Claude Code's current default hook timeout (it used to be 60s and may be longer now). If it's 10 minutes, the case for the timeout gets stronger. If it's still 60s, it gets weaker.

content.text:
The screenshot in the PR is just your passing test run, so I assume you mean the reporter's July comment about stuck processes piling up. That point is real, but it doesn't support this PR as much as it first seems to.

**What they said:** they found 14 stuck `entire hooks …` processes, mostly from the `stop` and `session-end` hooks. Every session leaked one on exit. In April some were more than 18 hours old.

**Why that's a weak argument for the PR:**
- **The PR doesn't cover those hooks.** It only adds a timeout to SessionStart, and the leaked processes came from Stop and SessionEnd. The reporter flagged exactly this gap.
- **A timeout may not clean them up anyway.** Those Claude hooks already had Claude Code's default timeout, and the processes still survived for hours. So that timeout stopped Claude from waiting but didn't kill the stuck process. A 5s timeout would most likely leave them behind the same way. I haven't verified this.
- **Git hooks leak too.** `git commit` hung in every repo with Entire enabled, and git hooks have no timeout at all.

**What it does support:** the stall is real. Every Claude start in an affected repo waits on a stuck hook. That's the part a SessionStart timeout fixes, and it's the "the side tool shouldn't block the main tool" argument from before. It's a reasonable reason to have the fix, but it doesn't cover the leaks or the commit hangs.

**How to settle it:** add a fake hook that just sleeps, with `timeout: 5`, and check whether Claude Code kills the process or leaves it running. If it kills it, a timeout on every Entire hook would also stop the leak, which makes a much stronger case for a reworked PR. If it doesn't, the timeout only speeds up startup.

Want me to run that check? Or, if you meant a different part of the issue, point me at it.

content.text:
The timeout works, so I'd go with rewriting the PR (option 2a) rather than closing it. With the timeout, Claude killed the stuck hook and carried on. Without it, Claude was still blocked after 40 seconds.

**How I tested it:** I used Claude Code 2.1.296 in a scratch directory. A fake `entire` on `PATH` just slept for 120s, and the hook command had the exact same `sh -c '…; exec entire hooks claude-code session-start'` shape that production uses.

| Setup | What happened |
|---|---|
| `timeout: 3` | Claude killed the hook process about 3s after it started, then replied and exited normally. The process was gone before Claude exited, so the timeout killed it, not Claude shutting down. |
| No timeout (Claude's default) | Claude was still stuck waiting on the hook after 40s. I killed the hook myself at that point, and Claude only finished afterwards. |

**This corrects what I said earlier.** I guessed that Claude's default timeout had stopped waiting but left the processes running, so a shorter timeout wouldn't clean them up either. The test shows otherwise: without a timeout Claude really does block, and with one it kills the process. The reporter's 14 stuck processes are more likely what's left when people give up and quit Claude while a hook is stuck. That's an inference, but it fits.

So the case for the fix is stronger than I made it sound:
- Claude stays usable when `entire` can't start.
- Stuck hook processes get killed instead of piling up, as long as every Entire hook has a timeout, not just SessionStart.

**Limit of the test:** my fake hung in `sleep`, while the real one hangs inside macOS's exec check (`_dyld_start`). The reporter was able to kill those processes by hand, so I expect Claude's kill to work on them too, but I haven't tested that exact state. The scratch files are deleted and no test processes are left running.

**Next step:** close #1237 and open a fresh PR from current `main` that:
- sets SessionStart to 5s;
- sets Stop and SessionEnd to a larger budget, about 30s, since they do real work;
- adds the timeout to existing installs only where none is set;
- leaves the git-hook hangs to the follow-up the reporter offered.

Hook timeouts: a flat 30s is wrong in both directions, and the cap is doing telemetry's job by Soph 2026-08-24T15:25:40Z

Two questions came up from a real timeout report: how did we land on a flat 30s for Codex hooks, and should it differ per hook? The history turns out to matter, and it reframes the report.

## Where 30s came from

Introduced in 433103a7c (2026-08-10, *feat(codex): finalize sessions via Codex's SessionEnd hook*). The constant documents its own scope:

> `defaultHookTimeoutSec` is the timeout Entire configures for Codex hooks that run between turns, **where Codex allows up to its standard 600s.**

So **30s is our own conservative default with 20× headroom available**, not a platform limit. That matters for the report that prompted this: a 65MB Codex rollout took 30.203s in the Stop hook, got its process tree killed, and left the checkpoint's final full-transcript rewrite incomplete. That user wasn't hitting a Codex constraint — he was hitting our round number.

There is no design record beyond that comment, and it reads as a sensible default chosen while wiring SessionEnd rather than a measured decision. Nothing was known to run long at the time.

**We already differentiate once, and it's the well-reasoned one.** `SessionEndTimeoutSec = 3`, because Codex clamps SessionEnd to `SESSION_END_MAX_TIMEOUT_SEC = 3` and warns on every startup if a config asks for more, so we request exactly the ceiling. It even carries a 1s internal gap to cover `sh` startup, the `command -v` PATH walk, and loading a ~66MB binary before our own clock starts. That's the standard to aim for.

The `managedHook` table already has a per-entry `timeout` field, so **differentiation is structurally supported and simply unused** — everything but SessionEnd takes the default.

## The tension

A hard kill is itself a failure: if a few more seconds would have completed the write, the timeout caused the damage it was meant to prevent. But raising it means we hear about degradation less often — the timeout is currently doing double duty as an accidental telemetry channel.

**The second half does not survive the data.** Across 287 real hook spans:

| threshold | spans over | share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1.5s (the WARN threshold from #1984) | 274 | 95.5% |
| 5s | 39 | 13.6% |
| 10s | 3 | 1.0% |
| 15s | 1 | 0.3% |
| **30s (the cap)** | **0** | **0%** |

The cap fired **zero** times. The WARN traces fired 274 times, each with a full step breakdown. We are not trading signal for silence — we already have ~274× more signal than the timeout provides.

And the report that started this did not come from the timeout. It came from a user noticing his agent break and taking the trouble to say so. That is the worst channel available: it needs user pain *plus* user effort, and it is silent for everyone who shrugs. Nobody reports the 12–16s pre-push runs, and those are where a rising trend shows up first.

**The real gap is that the signal never leaves the machine.** The traces already sit in every user's `.entire/logs/entire.log` at WARN and nothing brings them to us. Worth fixing independently of the timeouts.

## Measured cost per hook

| hook | n | p50 | p90 | max | headroom vs 30s |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `pre-push` | 94 | 4622ms | 7644ms | **16394ms** | **1.8×** |
| `stop` | 89 | 2331ms | 3074ms | 9838ms | 3.0× |
| `post-commit` | 93 | 2313ms | 3908ms | 5906ms | 5.1× |
| `user-prompt-submit` | 3 | 24ms | 2123ms | 2123ms | 14× |
| `prepare-commit-msg` | 3 | 11ms | 13ms | 13ms | 2300× |
| `commit-msg`, `session-start`, `session-end` | 3, 1, 1 | ~0–12ms | | | — |

One flat number is wrong in both directions. `pre-push` has been observed at 16.4s — 1.8× from the cliff, and it is network-bound, so someone else's slow link closes that gap with no code change on our side. Meanwhile `prepare-commit-msg` gets 30s for 10ms of work.

## Proposal

**1. Per-hook caps**, using the table field that already exists.

- `pre-push` → 120s. It waits on a remote; its worst case is set by someone else's network, and a kill mid-push is the worst failure mode we have.
- `stop`, `post-commit` → 60s. Both scale with transcript size and accumulated session count. #2107 helped; the ceiling still should not be 3× a *measured* max.
- `prepare-commit-msg`, `commit-msg`, `session-start` → 10s. Still 500×+ observed cost, and a tight bound here is a genuine safety property: these run *inside* the user's git operations, where a hang is far more visible than a slow Stop.

**2. A soft budget under each hard cap**, generalizing what SessionEnd already does. `sessionEndBudget` is deliberately held below `SessionEndTimeoutSec` so "Entire stops itself cleanly instead of being terminated part-way through a condense." On breach: warn, complete or degrade gracefully, and never get killed mid-write.

**3. Persist and surface the breach.** `CaptureDegradedAt` is the precedent — set in `lifecycle.go:1905`, cleared by the next healthy turn, and printed by `status.go:608` as "capture degraded …: status scan over budget … (see 'entire doctor logs')". Same shape for a hook that crossed its soft budget.

Together that is strictly *more* signal than today: it fires on the approach rather than only at the cliff, and for every user rather than only the ones who complain.

## Open questions

- **Are these the right numbers?** They come from one developer's corpus across 95 log files. A 65MB Codex session is already outside it, so the tail is under-sampled.
- **Where should the soft threshold sit** relative to the hard cap — a fixed gap like SessionEnd's 1s, or a fraction?
- **Do we want aggregate visibility** (telemetry, or an `entire status` nudge to send a bundle), or is local-only the deliberate privacy stance? This is the decision that actually determines whether raising caps costs us anything.
- **Per-hook values become hook-config drift**, so `dropStaleEntireHooks` will rewrite existing users' `hooks.json` on their next `enable`. Correct behaviour, but it lands in everyone's config.
- **Do other agents need the same treatment?** This is Codex-specific today; Claude Code, Cursor, Pi and OpenCode have their own hook-timeout stories that nobody has surveyed.

## Not the point

Raising a ceiling is not a latency fix. User-visible slowness should come from making the work fast — #2091 tracks the remaining items (`process_sessions`, the doubled compact-transcript generation, the un-instrumented sentinel). Timeouts are the backstop, and the argument here is only about the backstop failing badly rather than gracefully.

content.text:
Yes, but it's the opposite problem. Claude's hooks have no time limit, so they can hang. Pi's hooks already have a limit, and it may be too tight.

**How Pi runs hooks:** Entire installs a generated extension (`cmd/entire/cli/agent/pi/entire_extension.ts:34-37` on `main`). It runs every hook with Node's `execFile(..., { timeout: 10000 })`, so each hook gets 10 seconds. That has been in place since Pi support was added on 2026-05-09. After 10s Node kills the process and Pi carries on. So the #1065 hang can't block Pi the way it blocks Claude.

**Pi's actual risk is the flat 10s limit.** Issue #2115 (Soph, open since 2026-08-24) tracks this kind of problem. It started with Codex's flat 30s timeout killing a Stop hook that was in the middle of writing a large transcript. Its measurements:

| Hook | p90 | Max |
|---|---|---|
| `stop` (Pi's `agent_end`) | 3.1s | **9.8s** |
| `session-start` | ~ms | ~ms |

Pi's `agent_end` gets the same 10s as everything else, which is barely above that 9.8s max. A large session could get killed partway through saving its checkpoint. The issue says outright that Claude's and Pi's timeouts "have their own hook-timeout stories that nobody has surveyed".

There's one thing I couldn't verify: the reporter also saw leaked processes from Pi sessions. If Pi exits before a hook's 10s limit runs out, the stuck hook process may be left running. Checking that needs Pi installed, which I didn't do.

**What this means for #1237:**
- **Keep it Claude-only.** Pi's problem is a different fix in different code (the generated `.ts` extension). It belongs with #2115, and a comment there pointing out Pi's flat 10s would be useful.
- **Change the numbers I suggested, based on #2115's data:**
  - SessionStart: **10s** rather than 5s. That's still far above its measured cost, and it leaves room for the slow first launch after an upgrade.
  - Stop: **60s** rather than 30s. The 30s I proposed would bring Codex's failure to Claude. 60s still stops an endless hang but won't cut off a real save.
  - SessionEnd: check what Claude allows. Codex caps SessionEnd at 3s, and Claude may have a similar ceiling.
- **Mention #2115 in the PR description,** so reviewers see the timeouts follow the same per-hook reasoning.

content.text:
Here's the plan for the edits. Nothing in the repo is changed yet.

**Problem**

On `main`, none of Entire's Claude hooks have a time limit (`hooks.go:598` says so on purpose). When the `entire` binary can't start (#1065, macOS stuck before `main()`), every Claude hook that waits for its result stalls. That covers session start, every prompt, every turn end, and subagent and skill tool calls. My test today showed Claude still blocked after 40s with no timeout set. With `timeout` set, Claude killed the hook and carried on.

**Root cause**

The hang happens before any Entire code runs, so only Claude can enforce the limit, through the per-hook `timeout` in `settings.json`. We never set it.

**Proposed change** (rewrite the PR branch from current `origin/main`)

1. **One new field, `timeout`, in the `entireSimpleHook` table** (`hooks.go:203`), plus the same for the Task/Skill tool hooks. The values follow #2115's measurements:

   | Hook | Timeout | Why |
   |---|---|---|
   | session-start, user-prompt-submit, subagent-start, pre-task | **10s** | Measured in milliseconds, max about 2s. They block the user directly. |
   | stop, stop-failure, subagent-stop, post-task | **60s** | They save checkpoints and scale with transcript size. Measured max for stop is 9.8s. |
   | session-end | **none** | Claude already gives exit hooks only a short time. Setting one makes Claude wait *longer* on exit, which is what `455b6edc7` used it for. |

2. **Existing installs:** on `entire enable`, fill in the timeout on Entire's own entries when none is set, and write the file even if no hook was added (same idea as `staleDropped`). If a user set a timeout themselves, leave it alone. That fixes the "overwrites the user's value" problem in the current PR.
3. Rewrite the comments at `hooks.go:598` and `types.go:31`, which currently say Entire never sets a timeout.
4. **Tests first** (`hooks_test.go`), then the code:
   - a fresh install writes the right timeout for each hook, and none for session-end;
   - an old install without timeouts gets them filled in and the file is rewritten;
   - a timeout the user set is preserved;
   - running enable a second time doesn't rewrite the file.
5. **Check it against real Claude:** run `entire enable` in a temp repo with a hanging fake `entire`, start Claude, and confirm it starts and the hook process gets killed. Then `mise run fmt && mise run lint` and the claudecode tests.

**Scope and trade-offs**
- **Option A, every blocking hook (recommended).** A stuck binary hangs every hook the same way, and it's one extra table column. Covering only session-start would leave the problem in place on every prompt and every turn.
- **Option B, session-start and stop only.** Smaller diff and closer to the original PR, but prompts still hang.
- **Risk:** a stop hook running past 60s would be killed partway through a save. That's 6x the measured max, and the same trade-off #2115 proposes.
- **Not included:** git hooks (the reporter's follow-up), Pi (belongs in #2115), and having `entire doctor` flag missing timeouts as stale. That last one would nudge existing users to re-run enable, but it's a separate behavior change.

**Git steps, each needing your approval**
1. Reset the local branch `fix-claude-hook-launch-timeout` onto `origin/main`. Your old commit `8f34c2ef4` stays on the PR's remote branch.
2. Later, force-push and update the PR description. I'll show you the text first.

Approve option A (or B), and is the branch reset OK?

Improve the quality of changed code without hunting for correctness bugs. Review only the selected diff, then apply the safe cleanup findings directly.

## 1. Gather the review diff

Use an explicit PR number, branch, commit range, or file path when the user supplies one. Otherwise:

1. Run `git status --short` to detect working-tree changes.
2. Try `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD`.
3. If no upstream exists, use `git diff main...HEAD`; if `main` is unavailable, use `git diff HEAD~1`.
4. If the range diff is empty or the working tree has tracked changes, also run `git diff HEAD` and include it in scope.
5. Include relevant untracked source files reported by `git status` when they are part of the requested change.

Keep the exact unified diff available to pass to every reviewer. Do not silently expand the review to unrelated existing code.

## 2. Run four cleanup reviews concurrently

Launch four independent review subagents before awaiting any result. Give every reviewer the same unified diff, the repository location, the instruction not to edit files, and exactly one angle below. If the runtime cannot host four subagents at once, keep every available slot busy and launch the remaining reviewer as soon as a slot opens.

Each reviewer may inspect adjacent code and shared modules to validate a finding. Require only high-confidence findings in this format:

- file and line
- one-line summary
- concrete cost: what is duplicated, wasted, retained, or harder to maintain
- proposed simpler form or existing helper

An empty result is valid. Reviewers must not report correctness bugs or speculative behavior changes.

### Reuse

Find code in the diff that reimplements an existing abstraction. Search shared utilities and files adjacent to the change. Name the existing helper, type, or pattern that should be reused and explain the duplication removed.

### Simplification

Find complexity introduced by the diff: redundant or derivable state, near-copy-paste, avoidable branching or nesting, indirection without leverage, and dead code left behind. Name the simpler equivalent.

### Efficiency

Find unnecessary work introduced by the diff: repeated computation or I/O, avoidably sequential independent work, and blocking work added to startup or hot paths. Also check long-lived objects built from closures: captured environments can retain the entire enclosing scope, so prefer a class or struct that stores only the required fields when that materially reduces retention. Name the cheaper alternative.

### Altitude

Check whether the change operates at the right abstraction level. Flag symptom patches or special cases layered on shared infrastructure when a smaller general change to the underlying mechanism would remove the need for them. Name that deeper change, but keep recommendations within the review scope.

## 3. Triage and apply

Wait for all four reviews, then merge findings that point to the same line or underlying mechanism. Inspect the cited code before accepting a finding.

Before editing, show the user each accepted problem, why the current code causes
it, and the proposed cleanup. Include the scope and any meaningful tradeoffs.
Wait for the user's explicit approval of the proposed cleanups. The request to
run `/simplify` does not replace this checkpoint.

Apply each remaining cleanup when it:

- preserves intended behavior and public contracts;
- stays within or immediately adjacent to the reviewed change;
- clearly improves reuse, simplicity, efficiency, or abstraction level; and
- does not overwrite unrelated user work.

Skip false positives and any suggestion that would change intended behavior or require a broad refactor outside the diff. Record a short reason for every skipped finding; do not debate the reviewer.

Run focused formatting, tests, or checks appropriate to the touched code. Review the final diff to ensure the cleanup did not broaden scope.

## 4. Report

Briefly summarize the cleanups applied and the verification performed. List skipped findings with their reasons, or state that none were skipped. If no worthwhile findings remain, say the changed code was already clean under these four criteria.

content.text:
All four reviews are back. The useful findings all point the same way: treat the timeout as data on each hook, and have one function that adds or updates a hook. I'd apply them in the rewrite rather than to this old commit. Nothing is edited yet.

**Accepted findings** (I checked each one against the code)

1. **SessionStart has its own install path** (`hooks.go:138-148`). Problem: it gets a one-off `sessionStartTimeout` variable, a `localDev` branch, and its own function, while the other six hooks use check-then-add. Only SessionStart can patch an existing entry, so every hook that later needs a timeout would need another special case. Fix: give each hook definition a `timeout` value. Current `main` already has that table (`entireSimpleHooks()`), so it's one extra field, which is what the plan above does.
2. **Three functions where one is enough** (`hooks.go:436-445`). `addHookToMatcher` calls `addHookToMatcherWithTimeout`, which only forwards to `ensureHookInMatcherWithTimeout`, and grep shows nothing else calls the middle one. Fix: a single `ensureHookInMatcher(matchers, matcher, cmd, timeout) (matchers, changed)` that replaces each check-then-add pair. Drop "WithTimeout" from the name since there's nothing to tell it apart from.
3. **The two new tests repeat a loop** (`hooks_test.go:456-470`, `504-517`). Each copies the hook-search loop that `assertHookExists` (`hooks_test.go:590`) already has. Fix: a `findHook` helper that `assertHookExists` also uses, and one table-driven test (fresh install, old install without a timeout, timeout set by the user). Also delete the precondition check at `:491-494`, which only confirms that the JSON the test just wrote has no timeout.

**Skipped**
- **Extract a `findHookIndex` helper** (reuse #3). With fix 2 in place, the install path stops calling `hookCommandExistsWithMatcher`, so most of that duplication goes away. Whatever is left isn't worth a new helper.
- **Efficiency:** no findings. The diff adds no extra I/O or work on startup.

**Why not edit the current branch:** this commit is built around `localDev`, which `main` no longer has, and the approved plan rewrites the branch from `origin/main`. Cleaning it up now would be thrown away. All three fixes carry over directly into the rewrite.

So the earlier question still decides everything:
1. **Option A** (timeouts on every blocking hook) or **B** (SessionStart and Stop only)?
2. OK to reset the local branch onto `origin/main`? Your old commit stays on the PR's remote branch.

Once you approve, I'll write the tests first, then the code with these three fixes, then check it against real Claude.

content.text:
I recommend **option A**, and yes to the branch reset.

**Why A:**
- **When the binary is stuck, it's stuck for every hook.** In the #1065 state, every `entire` launch hangs, not just session start. With option B, Claude would start fine and then freeze on your first prompt, because user-prompt-submit still has no time limit. That fixes nothing the user can actually feel.
- **It costs about the same as B.** With the timeout on each hook in the table, A is one value per row. B would be the same code with blanks in most rows.
- **The numbers are backed by data.** 10s for the quick hooks and 60s for the ones that save checkpoints both sit well above #2115's measured max, so a healthy hook won't get killed.
- **Session-end stays as it is.** Claude already gives it only a short time on exit, and setting a timeout would make Claude wait *longer*.

**Why reset:** the old commit is built on `localDev`, which no longer exists, so rebasing would mostly mean resolving conflicts in dead code. Rewriting from `origin/main` is cleaner. Your old commit is still on the PR's remote branch if you want it back.

**What happens after you say go:**
1. Reset the local branch onto `origin/main`.
2. Write the table-driven tests first and confirm they fail.
3. Add the timeout column, the single `ensureHookInMatcher`, and the update logic for existing installs, and fix the two outdated comments.
4. Run fmt, lint, and the claudecode tests, then run real Claude against a hanging fake `entire`.
5. Show you the diff and a draft PR description. The force-push waits for your separate approval.

Go ahead with A and the reset?

I've stopped: the auto-mode safety check blocked moving the branch, twice. Nothing has changed. Your branch, your commit, and the untracked docs are exactly as they were.

**What I was trying to do:** point the local branch `fix-claude-hook-launch-timeout` at `upstream/main` so the rewrite starts clean. I tried `git reset --hard`, then the safer backup-branch plus `git checkout -B`, and both were refused as destructive. I won't try to get around it.

**Why it's actually safe**
- Your old commit `8f34c2ef4` is on the PR's remote branch (`ddae46d` contains it).
- The working tree has no tracked changes, only your three untracked `docs/*.html` files, and none of their paths exist on `upstream/main`.
- One correction: `origin` is your fork, which is 24 commits behind. The rewrite will build on `upstream/main` (`3780a5c31`). None of those 24 commits touch the Claude hook code, so my earlier analysis still holds.

**To unblock,** run this yourself (the `!` runs it in this session):

```
! git branch backup/fix-claude-hook-launch-timeout-8f34c2e 8f34c2ef4 && git checkout -B fix-claude-hook-launch-timeout upstream/main
```

That keeps a local backup branch and moves the branch without touching the untracked files. Once it's done, I'll continue with the tests first.

content.text:
Fair question. Here's the honest answer.

**Why I wanted the reset:** your PR's code is built on an old version of `hooks.go` (with `localDev`). The fix has to be written against today's `main`, so I wanted the branch to start from `main` with your old change gone.

**But a reset isn't needed for that, and it brings two costs:**
- it moves the branch, which is what the safety check blocked;
- it needs a **force-push** later, which rewrites the PR's history.

**A better way that removes nothing:**
1. Fast-forward your local branch to the PR's current head (`ddae46d`). Local is just behind it, so nothing gets rewritten.
2. Merge `upstream/main` into it. That's how the PR has been kept current already: `ddae46d` and `a88bd7a` are merges from `main`. Where `hooks.go` conflicts, take `main`'s version, since the old approach is being replaced anyway.
3. Add the new fix as a normal commit on top.
4. Push normally, with no force-push.

Afterwards, the PR's diff against `main` shows only the new fix, the history stays intact, and the PR still links to #1065. If the repo squash-merges, the extra commits don't matter at all.

All of these are ordinary git operations I can run myself. I'll show you the diff before pushing, and the push still waits for your approval.

Should I do it that way?

sed -i '' 's/sleep 300/sleep 1800/' $S/hangbin/entire
cd $S/repo
now() { python3 -c 'import time;print(time.time())'; }
t0=$(now)
( PATH=$S/hangbin:$PATH claude -p --model haiku "reply with just: ok" > $S/claude_out 2>&1; now > $S/claude_end ) &
seen=""
while :; do
  el=$(python3 -c "print(int($(now)-$t0))")
  [ -f $S/hooks.log ] && while read name pid ts; do
    case " $seen " in *" $pid "*) continue;; esac
    if ! kill -0 $pid 2>/dev/null; then echo "$name $pid $ts $(now)" >> $S/deaths.log; seen="$seen $pid"; fi
  done < $S/hooks.log
  [ -f $S/claude_end ] && break
  [ $el -gt 420 ] && { echo "claude still running after 420s"; break; }
  sleep 0.5
done
echo "claude end: $([ -f $S/claude_end ] && python3 -c "print(round($(cat $S/claude_end)-$t0,1))" || echo n/a)s"
while read name pid ts; do
  d=$(grep " $pid " $S/deaths.log | awk '{print $4}')
  if [ -n "$d" ]; then echo "  $name started +$(python3 -c "print(round($ts-$t0,1))")s, died +$(python3 -c "print(round($d-$t0,1))")s (lived $(python3 -c "print(round($d-$ts,1))")s)"
  else echo "  $name started +$(python3 -c "print(round($ts-$t0,1))")s, STILL ALIVE"; kill $pid 2>/dev/null; fi

( PATH=$S/hangbin:$PATH claude -p --model haiku "reply with just: ok" > $S/claude_out 2>&1; now > $S/claude_end ) &
seen=""
while :; do
  el=$(python3 -c "print(int($(now)-$t0))")
  [ -f $S/hooks.log ] && while read name pid ts; do
    case " $seen " in *" $pid "*) continue;; esac
    if ! kill -0 $pid 2>/dev/null; then echo "$name $pid $ts $(now)" >> $S/deaths.log; seen="$seen $pid"; fi
  done < $S/hooks.log
  [ -f $S/claude_end ] && break
  [ $el -gt 420 ] && { echo "claude still running after 420s"; break; }
  sleep 0.5
done
echo "claude end: $([ -f $S/claude_end ] && python3 -c "print(round($(cat $S/claude_end)-$t0,1))" || echo n/a)s"
while read name pid ts; do
  d=$(grep " $pid " $S/deaths.log | awk '{print $4}')
  if [ -n "$d" ]; then echo "  $name started +$(python3 -c "print(round($ts-$t0,1))")s, died +$(python3 -c "print(round($d-$t0,1))")s (lived $(python3 -c "print(round($d-$ts,1))")s)"
  else echo "  $name started +$(python3 -c "print(round($ts-$t0,1))")s, STILL ALIVE"; kill $pid 2>/dev/null; fi
done < $S/hooks.log
cat $S/claude_out | tail -3

content.text:
The fix is in place, and real Claude confirms it: when `entire` hangs, Claude kills the stuck hook at its timeout and carries on. Nothing is committed or pushed yet.

**What changed** (3 files, on top of a merge of `upstream/main`, no force-push needed):
- **`hooks.go`:**
  - each hook in the table now carries its own timeout: 10s for session-start, user-prompt-submit, subagent-start and pre-task; 60s for stop, stop-failure, subagent-stop and post-task; none for session-end;
  - `entire enable` adds the timeout to existing entries that have none, and leaves any timeout the user set themselves;
  - the comment that said Entire never sets timeouts is replaced.
- **`hooks_test.go`:** tests for each hook's timeout, for older installs getting the timeout added, for keeping a user's own value, and for a second install not rewriting the file. They also share one hook-lookup helper, from the cleanup review. Two existing tests that assumed "no timeouts" are updated.
- **`.claude/settings.json`:** the repo's own Claude config now includes the timeouts. A test checks this file matches what install writes.

**How I verified it**
- The new tests failed before the change and pass after it. The whole claudecode package passes.
- `mise run fmt` changed nothing, and `mise run lint` reports 0 issues.
- `mise run test` (the full unit suite) passed except one git-hook test in `strategy`. It was killed while the machine was busy with my Claude run, then passed 3 out of 3 on its own, and nothing in that package changed.
- **Real install:** `entire enable` in a throwaway repo wrote exactly these timeouts. After I removed them by hand, a second `enable` put them back and kept a timeout of 300 I'd set myself.
- **Real Claude with a hanging `entire`:** session-start was killed at 9.9s and user-prompt-submit at 10.1s. Stop was killed at 300.5s, matching the 300 I'd set on it during the previous check. Session-end was cut off by Claude's own exit limit at 1.5s, and Claude still answered.

**Not verified**
- The exact macOS "stuck in `_dyld_start`" state. My fake `entire` hung in `sleep` instead.
- The integration tests and the canary from `mise run check`. Those run before the commit.

**Small gap:** when `enable` only adds missing timeouts, it still prints "already installed". I left that alone because changing it would mean touching setup-wide output.

**Next, each step needs your go-ahead:**
1. Commit with: `fix(claude-code): time out Entire hooks so a stalled launch can't block Claude`
2. Push to your fork's branch (a normal push), then update the PR description. I'll show you the text first.

---
name: stale-entire-breaks-integration-tests
description: "Local integration test failures that pass in CI can come from an outdated Homebrew `entire` on PATH firing in test repos' git hooks"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 19717fad-3912-4238-a80e-79b2a3057ad2
  modified: 2026-10-13T09:57:54.146Z
---

Integration tests that run real git commands (e.g. `git rebase`) fire the test repo's installed hooks, which call `entire` from PATH, so they run `/opt/homebrew/bin/entire` (Homebrew cask `entireio/tap/entire@nightly`), not the test-built binary. When the installed nightly is older than main, its hooks can corrupt session state, e.g. delete it. On 2026-10-13 this made `TestManualCommit_MidSessionRebaseFollowsHead` and `TestCheckpointDelete_LeftoverDeletedIDNeverReceivesNewWork` fail locally while CI, which has no `entire` installed, passed.

**Why:** Hours were spent ruling out env vars, git config and ctime before finding this.
**How to apply:** If integration tests fail locally but pass on CI for the same SHA, first check `entire version` against main. Fix with `brew upgrade --cask entireio/tap/entire@nightly`, or put a fresh `go build ./cmd/entire` first on PATH.

---

fixes #1065

Gives each of Entire's Claude Code hooks a timeout, so Claude Code kills a stalled `entire` launch and keeps going instead of waiting on it.

#### why

In #1065, macOS blocks `entire` before Go `main()` runs (`_dyld_start`), so nothing inside the binary can time out. Without a hook `timeout`, Claude Code kept waiting on the stuck hook (still blocked after 40s in testing), and the reporter saw stuck hook processes pile up across sessions. With a `timeout` set, Claude Code kills the hook process and continues.

#### what changed

- Each entry in the Claude hook table now carries its own timeout:
  - **10s** for hooks that only record state and that Claude blocks startup or prompts on: `session-start`, `user-prompt-submit`, `subagent-start`, `pre-task`.
  - **60s** for hooks that write checkpoint data, whose cost grows with transcript size: `stop`, `stop-failure`, `subagent-stop`, `post-task`.
  - **None** for `session-end`. Claude Code already gives exit hooks only a short time, and an explicit timeout would make it wait longer.
- `entire enable` adds the timeout to existing Entire hooks that have none, so current users get it on their next enable. A timeout the user set themselves is kept.
- The repo's own `.claude/settings.json` is regenerated to match.

The values follow the per-hook measurements in #2115: `stop` max 9.8s, and `session-start` / `user-prompt-submit` max about 2s.

#### test plan

- [x] New tests: each hook's timeout on a fresh install, timeouts added to an existing install, a user-set timeout kept, and a second install not rewriting the file.
- [x] `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/agent/claudecode/...`
- [x] `mise run fmt && mise run lint`
- [x] `mise run test:e2e:canary`
- [x] Manual check with the real binary and real Claude Code, using a fake `entire` on `PATH` that hangs forever:
  - `session-start` was killed at 9.9s and `user-prompt-submit` at 10.1s.
  - `session-end` was cut off by Claude's exit limit at 1.5s, and Claude still answered.
  - After the timeouts were removed by hand, `entire enable` added them back and kept a user-set value.

#### not in scope

- Git hooks (`prepare-commit-msg`, `post-commit`, ...) can still hang `git commit` in this state. The reporter offered a follow-up for that.
- Pi already applies a flat 10s timeout in its generated extension. Whether that suits each Pi hook is better tracked in #2115.
